Abbreviations and acronyms used in the document include the following: AMK: Amikacin BDQ: Bedaquiline BPaL: A combination of bedaquiline, pretomanid, and linezolid BPaLM: A combination of bedaquiline, pretomanid, linezolid, and moxifloxacin CFZ: Clofazimine DCS: D-cycloserine DLM: Delamanid DR-TB: Drug-resistant tuberculosis DST: Drug-susceptibility testing EMB: Ethambutol ETO: Ethionamide FQ: Fluoroquinolone HIV: Human immunodeficiency virus Hr-TB: Isoniazid-resistant, rifampicin-susceptible tuberculosis INH: Isoniazid LF-LAM: Lateral-flow urine lipoarabinomannan assay LFX: Levofloxacin LMIC: Lowand middle-income countries LZD: Linezolid M. tuberculosis: Mycobacterium tuberculosis MDR/RR-TB: Multidrug-resistant or rifampicin-resistant tuberculosis MDR-TB: Multidrug-resistant tuberculosis MXF: Moxifloxacin NAAT: Nucleic acid amplification test NGS: Next-generation sequencing Pa: Pretomanid PHC: Primary health care POC: Point of care PPV: Positive predictive value Pre-XDR-TB: Pre-extensively drug-resistant tuberculosis PZA: Pyrazinamide RIF: Rifampicin R&D: Research and development RR-TB: Rifampicin-resistant tuberculosis TB: Tuberculosis TPP: Target product profile USA: United States of America WHO: World Health Organization WRD: WHO-recommended rapid diagnostic XDR-TB: Extensively drug-resistant tuberculosis Drug resistance testing, also known as drug-susceptibility testing (DST), involves in vitro testing of Mycobacterium tuberculosis complex strains. This can be done using molecular or genotypic techniques to detect mutations that confer resistance or through phenotypic methods to determine susceptibility to specific drugs. Isoniazid-resistant, rifampicin-susceptible tuberculosis (Hr-TB) refers to strains of Mycobacterium tuberculosis complex that are resistant to isoniazid (INH) but remain susceptible to rifampicin (RIF). Rifampicin-resistant tuberculosis (RR-TB) is caused by strains resistant to RIF, which may also include multidrug-resistant TB (MDR-TB) or resistance to other first-line or second-line TB medications. MDR-TB is defined as resistance to at least both RIF and INH. Pre-extensively drug-resistant tuberculosis (pre-XDR-TB) is caused by strains that meet the definition of MDR/RR-TB and are also resistant to at least one fluoroquinolone (FQ), such as levofloxacin (LFX) or moxifloxacin (MXF). Extensively drug-resistant tuberculosis (XDR-TB) is caused by strains that meet the definition of MDR/RR-TB and are resistant to at least one FQ (LFX or MXF) and at least one additional Group A drug, such as bedaquiline (BDQ) or linezolid (LZD). Point-of-care (POC) tests are diagnostic tools that do not require specialized infrastructure, such as electricity, equipment, or cold chain storage, and can be used in healthcare settings without laboratories. These tests are simple to perform and do not require specialized skills. Examples include dipstick or lateral-flow formats. Near-POC tests may involve instruments, preferably battery-operated, and require minimal infrastructure. An example is a portable nucleic acid amplification test (NAAT) platform. Low-complexity assays, such as cartridge-based NAATs, can be performed in microscopy centers or basic health clinics with minimal laboratory infrastructure and staff with basic technical skills. Tuberculosis (TB) remains one of the deadliest infectious diseases globally. Despite progress in diagnosing and treating TB cases, global TB targets remain unmet. In 2022, 5 million people were diagnosed with TB, the highest number in nearly three decades. However, a significant gap persists between the estimated number of people who develop TB annually and those who are diagnosed. Efforts to close these gaps have been made, but there is still a need for innovative tools, including novel diagnostics, to improve case identification, detect drug resistance, and guide treatment initiation. The World Health Organization (WHO) published its first high-priority target product profiles (TPPs) for new TB diagnostics in April 2014. These TPPs outlined technical specifications and operational characteristics important to end users, aiming to expedite the development of products addressing the most urgent public health needs. Since then, WHO has updated these targets to account for novel technologies, evolving needs, and the transition of tools from research to clinical use. The updated TPPs align with WHO’s strategic priorities, including the End TB Strategy (2016–2035) and universal health coverage goals. The updated TPPs include definitions for POC and near-POC tests and relate these to low-complexity diagnostic technologies. The rapid diagnostic TPP does not differentiate between sputum-based and non-sputum-based tests, as long as the diagnostic tool meets the required target. For the first time, a model-based approach was used to inform discussions on the performance and cost per test of new diagnostics. Stakeholder consultations, including Delphi processes and public calls, informed the revisions. The updated TPPs aim to guide the next five years of TB diagnostic development and advance the field. WHO expects these revisions to inform and guide stakeholders, including diagnostic manufacturers, product development partnerships, academics, funding agencies, and others involved in TB diagnostics. The TPPs aim to align R&D efforts with the needs of TB communities and global priorities, enabling rapid detection of Mycobacterium tuberculosis and drug resistance at the most basic levels of care. They also foster collaboration and coordination in developing novel diagnostic approaches. The present document supersedes the 2014 TPPs and incorporates updates on next-generation drug-susceptibility testing (DST) released in 2021.
